source_regions.S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1: For probability measures P and Q on a common measurable space, their total variation distance is \operatorname{TV}(P,Q):=\sup_{B}|P(B)-Q(B)|=\frac{1}{2}\int|p-q|\,d\lambda, where the supremum ranges over measurable sets, and p and q are the densities of P and Q with respect to any common dominating measure \lambda. In particular, |\mathbb{E}_{P}h-\mathbb{E}_{Q}h|\leq\operatorname{TV}(P,Q) for every measurable function h taking values in [0,1].
source_regions.S2.p2: Let O(n):=\{O\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}:O^{\top}O=I_{n}\} denote the real orthogonal group, equipped with Haar probability measure. It has two components, \{\det O=+1\}, \{\det O=-1\}, and each have Haar probability 1/2. For b\in\{-1,+1\}, we write \mu_{n,b} for Haar probability measure conditioned on \det O=b.
source_regions.S3.SS1.p1: Fix \kappa\geq 4. Let 3\leq n\leq d be the block dimension and k:=\lfloor d/n\rfloor the number of blocks. In the proof of the main theorem, we choose n=2T+1, where T is the algorithm’s query budget. This choice applies when T\geq 1 and 2T+1\leq d. The remaining cases are treated separately. For O\in O(n), define A_{O}:=\frac{\kappa+1}{2}I_{n}-\frac{\kappa-1}{4}(O+O^{\top}). (4) For \bm{O}=(O_{1},\ldots,O_{k})\in O(n)^{k}, set A_{\bm{O}}:=\operatorname{diag}\bigl(A_{O_{1}},\ldots,A_{O_{k}},I_{d-kn}\bigr). (5)
source_regions.S3.SS1.p2: For each b\in\{-1,+1\}, draw O_{1},\ldots,O_{k} independently from \mu_{n,b}, and let \mathcal{D}_{b} denote the law of A_{\bm{O}}. Thus the orthogonal matrices share the same determinant sign.
source_regions.S3.SS1.p3: Writing P_{b}:=\mathbb{E}_{O\sim\mu_{n,b}}[N(0,A_{O}^{-1})] for the single-block target mixture, the averaged target under \mathcal{D}_{b} is \bar{\pi}_{b}:=\mathbb{E}_{A\sim\mathcal{D}_{b}}[\pi_{A}]=P_{b}^{\otimes k}\otimes N(0,I_{d-kn}). (6) When kn=d, the identity block and the final Gaussian factor are omitted.
source_regions.A2.SS2.p2: We first separate the single-block mixtures using a bounded radial test, and then amplify this separation across independent blocks. The single-block argument combines a cancellation identity for Gaussian normalization factors with two spherical Poisson identities. Throughout this section, n\geq 3, \kappa\geq 4, and O is Haar distributed on the full orthogonal group O(n). Write U:=O_{11}, let p_{O} be the density of N(0,A_{O}^{-1}), and let p_{b} be the density of P_{b}, for b\in\{-1,+1\}.
source_regions.A2.SS2.SSS2.p3: For \lambda\geq 0, let h_{\lambda}(x):=e^{-\lambda\|x\|^{2}} and define H(\lambda):=\mathbb{E}\left[\det(O)\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}h_{\lambda}(x)p_{O}(x)\,dx\right]. Since the two determinant components have Haar probability 1/2, H(\lambda)=\frac{1}{2}\left(\mathbb{E}_{P_{+1}}h_{\lambda}-\mathbb{E}_{P_{-1}}h_{\lambda}\right). As 0<h_{\lambda}\leq 1, it follows that \operatorname{TV}(P_{+1},P_{-1})\geq 2|H(\lambda)|. (20) We compute H(\lambda) and then choose \lambda>0.

neighboring_exclusions.A2.SS2.SSS2.p1: We distinguish P_{+1} and P_{-1} using a test of the form x\mapsto e^{-\lambda\|x\|^{2}}. After Gaussian integration and determinant cancellation, its expectation difference reduces to a spherical integral. The following identities evaluate that integral.
neighboring_exclusions.A2.SS2.SSS2.p2: Choosing \lambda so that these identities apply gives the following quantitative separation.
neighboring_exclusions.A2.SS2.SSS2.p4: For every Q\in O(n), conjugation preserves Haar measure and the determinant sign, while A_{QOQ^{\top}}=QA_{O}Q^{\top} and p_{QOQ^{\top}}(Qx)=p_{O}(x). Consequently, for every x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, \mathbb{E}[\det(O)p_{O}(x)]=\mathbb{E}[\det(O)p_{O}(\|x\|e_{1})]. At \|x\|e_{1}, the Gaussian exponent depends on O only through U, since e_{1}^{\top}A_{O}e_{1}=(\kappa+1-(\kappa-1)U)/2. Moreover, I_{n}\preceq A_{O}\preceq\kappa I_{n} gives the integrable bound h_{\lambda}(x)p_{O}(\|x\|e_{1})\leq\left(\frac{\kappa}{2\pi}\right)^{n/2}e^{-\|x\|^{2}/2}. Using |\det(O)|=1, Fubini’s theorem, and Gaussian integration, we obtain \displaystyle H(\lambda) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{n/2}}\mathbb{E}\left[\det(O)\sqrt{\det A_{O}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}e^{-[\kappa+1+4\lambda-(\kappa-1)U]\|x\|^{2}/4}\,dx\right] \displaystyle=2^{n/2}\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\det(O)\sqrt{\det A_{O}}}{(\kappa+1+4\lambda-(\kappa-1)U)^{n/2}}\right], where \int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}e^{-a\|x\|^{2}/4}\,dx=(4\pi/a)^{n/2} for a>0. The denominator is at least 2+4\lambda, so Lemma B.6 applies with h(u)=(\kappa+1+4\lambda-(\kappa-1)u)^{-n/2} and gives H(\lambda)=\frac{(-1)^{n-1}(\sqrt{\kappa}-1)^{n-1}}{2^{n/2}}\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{(\sqrt{\kappa}+1)U-(\sqrt{\kappa}-1)}{(\kappa+1+4\lambda-(\kappa-1)U)^{n/2}}\right]. (21) Since Oe_{1} is uniform on \mathbb{S}^{n-1}, Lemma A.1 applies to U.
neighboring_exclusions.A2.SS2.SSS2.p5: We now match the denominator with a positive multiple of 1+r^{2}-2rU. At \lambda=0, this matching gives r=(\sqrt{\kappa}-1)/(\sqrt{\kappa}+1), but H(0)=0 because both target distributions have total mass one. We therefore decrease r by a factor 1-1/n and set \displaystyle r \displaystyle:=\left(1-\frac{1}{n}\right)\frac{\sqrt{\kappa}-1}{\sqrt{\kappa}+1}, (22) \displaystyle\lambda \displaystyle:=\frac{\kappa-1}{8r}(1+r^{2})-\frac{\kappa+1}{4}=\frac{4n\sqrt{\kappa}+(\sqrt{\kappa}-1)^{2}}{8n(n-1)}. Then 0<r<1, \lambda>0, and \displaystyle\kappa+1+4\lambda-(\kappa-1)U \displaystyle=\frac{\kappa-1}{2r}(1+r^{2}-2rU) (23) \displaystyle=\frac{n(\sqrt{\kappa}+1)^{2}}{2(n-1)}(1+r^{2}-2rU). The two Poisson identities yield \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{(\sqrt{\kappa}+1)U-(\sqrt{\kappa}-1)}{(1+r^{2}-2rU)^{n/2}}\right] \displaystyle=\frac{(\sqrt{\kappa}+1)r-(\sqrt{\kappa}-1)}{1-r^{2}} \displaystyle=-\frac{\sqrt{\kappa}-1}{n(1-r^{2})}. Substitution into Eq. (21) gives \displaystyle H(\lambda) \displaystyle=\frac{(-1)^{n-1}(\sqrt{\kappa}-1)^{n-1}}{(\sqrt{\kappa}+1)^{n}}\left(1-\frac{1}{n}\right)^{n/2}\left(-\frac{\sqrt{\kappa}-1}{n(1-r^{2})}\right) (24) \displaystyle=\frac{(-1)^{n}}{n}\left(\frac{\sqrt{\kappa}-1}{\sqrt{\kappa}+1}\right)^{n}\frac{(1-1/n)^{n/2}}{1-r^{2}}.
neighboring_exclusions.A2.SS2.SSS2.p6: It remains to lower-bound the test gap. Since n/2\geq 1, convexity of t\mapsto t^{n/2} implies \left(1-\frac{1}{n}\right)^{n/2}\geq 1-\frac{n}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{n}=\frac{1}{2}. Also, \displaystyle n(1-r^{2}) \displaystyle=\frac{4n\sqrt{\kappa}}{(\sqrt{\kappa}+1)^{2}}+\left(\frac{\sqrt{\kappa}-1}{\sqrt{\kappa}+1}\right)^{2}\left(2-\frac{1}{n}\right) \displaystyle\leq\frac{4n\sqrt{\kappa}}{(\sqrt{\kappa}+1)^{2}}+2. Together with Eq. (20) and Eq. (24), these estimates give \displaystyle\operatorname{TV}(P_{+1},P_{-1}) \displaystyle\geq\frac{2}{n}\left(\frac{\sqrt{\kappa}-1}{\sqrt{\kappa}+1}\right)^{n}\frac{(1-1/n)^{n/2}}{1-r^{2}} \displaystyle\geq\frac{\left(\frac{\sqrt{\kappa}-1}{\sqrt{\kappa}+1}\right)^{n}}{2+\frac{4n\sqrt{\kappa}}{(\sqrt{\kappa}+1)^{2}}}. This proves the first claimed bound. For the second, \kappa\geq 4 implies \displaystyle\log\left(\frac{\sqrt{\kappa}+1}{\sqrt{\kappa}-1}\right) \displaystyle=2\int_{0}^{1/\sqrt{\kappa}}\frac{dt}{1-t^{2}} \displaystyle\leq\frac{2}{\sqrt{\kappa}(1-\kappa^{-1})}\leq\frac{8}{3\sqrt{\kappa}}\leq\frac{3}{\sqrt{\kappa}}. Hence ((\sqrt{\kappa}-1)/(\sqrt{\kappa}+1))^{n}\geq e^{-3n/\sqrt{\kappa}}. Using 1+t\leq e^{t}, we also have 2+\frac{4n\sqrt{\kappa}}{(\sqrt{\kappa}+1)^{2}}\leq 2+\frac{4n}{\sqrt{\kappa}}\leq 2e^{2n/\sqrt{\kappa}}. Therefore, \operatorname{TV}(P_{+1},P_{-1})\geq\frac{e^{-3n/\sqrt{\kappa}}}{2e^{2n/\sqrt{\kappa}}}=\frac{1}{2}e^{-5n/\sqrt{\kappa}}. ∎
